cards.r: chē dào shān qián bì yǒu lù
cards.mean: don't worry too early: a way out will appear when the time comes
cards.lit: when the cart reaches the foot of the mountain, there is bound to be a road

use.how: Said as a whole sentence to reassure someone, or oneself, who is worrying about a problem that cannot be solved yet: 别担心，车到山前必有路。

near.diff: Often said right after it as a pair; 船到桥头自然直 stresses that the problem straightens itself out, 车到山前必有路 that a way through will show up.

cards.cue: Your friend is losing sleep over what they will do if their visa runs out next summer, though nothing can be done about it yet. What do you say to calm them?

ctx.s: 别太担心了，{车到山前必有路}，总会有办法的。
ctx.en: Don't worry so much. Things will work out when we get there; there's always a way.

ctx.s: 工作丢了也不用慌，{车到山前必有路}。
ctx.en: No need to panic about losing your job. A way forward will turn up.

ctx.s: 你现在想那么多有什么用？{车到山前必有路}嘛。
ctx.en: What's the use of worrying about all that now? You'll find a way when the time comes.

ctx.s: 房东突然要收回房子，他却笑着说：“{车到山前必有路}，到时候再找呗。”
ctx.en: The landlord suddenly wanted the flat back, but he just laughed: "Something will turn up. I'll look for a place when I have to."

ctx.s: 钱还没凑齐，可爸爸说{车到山前必有路}，先把手续办了再说。
ctx.en: We still didn't have all the money, but Dad said a way would appear, so let's get the paperwork done first.

ctx.s: 当时谁也不知道公司能撑多久，大家只能相信{车到山前必有路}。
ctx.en: Back then nobody knew how long the company could hold on; all we could do was trust that a way out would come.

bad.s: 出发前一定要查好路线，{车到山前必有路}。
bad.en: (meant: be sure to plan your route carefully before you set off)
bad.why: The saying tells people not to worry ahead of time, so it cannot back up advice to plan ahead.

bad.s: 这道题很简单，{车到山前必有路}，你肯定会做。
bad.en: (meant: this question is easy, you can definitely do it)
bad.why: It is said about a real difficulty with no answer in sight yet, not about something that is easy.

cards.t: 三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮
cards.r: sān gè chòu pí jiang, dǐng gè zhū gě liàng
cards.mean: ordinary people pooling their ideas can outdo one genius
cards.lit: three smelly cobblers together are a match for Zhuge Liang, the wise strategist of the Three Kingdoms

use.how: Said as a whole sentence to suggest or praise putting heads together on a problem; slightly self-deprecating about the group: 大家一起想，三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮。

near.diff: 众人拾柴火焰高 is about many people adding their effort or strength; 三个臭皮匠 is about pooling ideas and thinking.

cards.cue: Nobody on your team is an expert, so instead of waiting for one clever person to crack the problem, you suggest everybody sit down and throw their ideas together.

ctx.s: 这个问题我想不出来，咱们一起想想吧，{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}。
ctx.en: I can't figure this out. Let's think about it together; several heads are better than one.

ctx.s: 别一个人发愁了，{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}，大家商量一下。
ctx.en: Don't fret over it on your own. Put a few ordinary heads together and they beat a genius, so let's talk it over.

ctx.s: 经理说：“{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}，每个人都说说自己的想法。”
ctx.en: The manager said: "Put our heads together and we can beat any genius. Everyone, tell us your ideas."

ctx.s: 这个办法是我们小组讨论出来的，你说是不是{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}？
ctx.en: Our group came up with this idea by talking it through. Doesn't that prove ordinary heads together can beat a genius?

ctx.s: 我们几个都不是专家，可{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}，最后还是把方案做出来了。
ctx.en: None of us were experts, but by pooling our ideas we got the plan done in the end.

ctx.s: 老师让学生分组讨论难题，因为她相信{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}。
ctx.en: The teacher had the students tackle hard problems in groups, because she believed ordinary minds together can outdo one brilliant one.

bad.s: 搬家的时候人多，{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}，一会儿就搬完了。
bad.en: (meant: lots of people helped with the move, so it was done in no time)
bad.why: It is about pooling ideas to solve a problem, not about many hands making physical work light.

bad.s: 他一个人就想出了好办法，真是{三个臭皮匠，顶个诸葛亮}。
bad.en: (meant: he came up with a great idea all by himself)
bad.why: The point is several ordinary people thinking together; it cannot praise one person working alone.

cards.r: yī fēn qián yī fēn huò
cards.mean: you get what you pay for: better goods cost more
cards.lit: one cent of money, one cent of goods: each bit you pay buys that much quality

use.how: Said about buying things: to justify a high price, or after something cheap turns out badly: 便宜的坏得快，一分钱一分货。

near.diff: 便宜没好货 only runs cheap things down; 一分钱一分货 says price and quality match either way, so it can also defend paying more.

cards.cue: Your friend complains that the bargain blender they bought online broke after two weeks, while yours, which cost three times as much, still works fine. What do you say?

ctx.s: 这双鞋贵是贵了点，但{一分钱一分货}，穿着很舒服。
ctx.en: These shoes are a bit pricey, but you get what you pay for; they're really comfortable.

ctx.s: 便宜的耳机用了一个月就坏了，真是{一分钱一分货}。
ctx.en: The cheap earphones broke after a month. You really do get what you pay for.

ctx.s: 店员笑着说：“{一分钱一分货}，这款手机的质量好多了。”
ctx.en: The shop assistant smiled: "You get what you pay for. This phone is much better made."

ctx.s: 你想花这么少的钱买到好沙发？{一分钱一分货}啊。
ctx.en: You want a good sofa for that little money? You get what you pay for, you know.

ctx.s: 装修的时候别光看价格，材料可是{一分钱一分货}的。
ctx.en: When you renovate, don't just look at the price; with materials, you get exactly what you pay for.

ctx.s: 他以前总买最便宜的，后来才明白{一分钱一分货}的道理。
ctx.en: He used to always buy the cheapest option; only later did he understand that you get what you pay for.

bad.s: 你学习越努力，成绩就越好，这就是{一分钱一分货}。
bad.en: (meant: the harder you study, the better your marks)
bad.why: It is about price and the quality of goods, not effort and reward; for that there is a different saying (yi fen gengyun, yi fen shouhuo).

bad.s: 这件衣服又便宜又好，真是{一分钱一分货}。
bad.en: (meant: this shirt is cheap and good, what a bargain)
bad.why: Cheap but good is the opposite of what it says: it links low price with low quality.

cards.r: shuō cáo cāo, cáo cāo dào
cards.mean: speak of the devil: the person just mentioned turns up
cards.lit: mention Cao Cao and Cao Cao arrives; Cao Cao was the powerful warlord of the Three Kingdoms era

use.how: An exclamation, said the moment someone who was just being talked about appears, calls or messages. Unlike the English, it carries no hint that the person is bad.

cards.cue: You and a friend are wondering aloud where your flatmate has got to, and at that very second the flatmate opens the front door.

ctx.s: {说曹操，曹操到}，你看，那不是老李吗？
ctx.en: Speak of the devil, look, isn't that Old Li?

ctx.s: 我们正说起小王，他就推门进来了，真是{说曹操，曹操到}！
ctx.en: We were just talking about Xiao Wang when he pushed the door open. Speak of the devil!

ctx.s: 刚提到她，她就打来电话了，{说曹操，曹操到}啊。
ctx.en: We'd only just mentioned her and she rang. Talk of the devil.

ctx.s: “哎，{说曹操，曹操到}！我们正聊你呢，快坐。”
ctx.en: "Hey, speak of the devil! We were just talking about you. Sit down."

ctx.s: 大家正在议论新来的经理，没想到{说曹操，曹操到}，他就站在门口。
ctx.en: Everyone was discussing the new manager when, speak of the devil, there he was standing in the doorway.

ctx.s: 我刚在群里问阿明去哪儿了，{说曹操，曹操到}，他马上就回了消息。
ctx.en: I'd just asked in the group chat where A-Ming had got to and, speak of the devil, he replied straight away.

bad.s: 会议九点开始，{说曹操，曹操到}，他九点准时到了。
bad.en: (meant: the meeting started at nine and he arrived right on time)
bad.why: It only fits when someone shows up just as people are talking about them, not when they simply arrive as scheduled.

bad.s: 他总是{说曹操，曹操到}，从来不迟到。
bad.en: (meant: he is always punctual and never late)
bad.why: It is an exclamation about one surprising moment, not a description of someone's habits or punctuality.

cards.r: tiān xià méi yǒu bù sàn de yán xí
cards.mean: every gathering must end; even good company has to part
cards.lit: under heaven there is no banquet that never breaks up

use.how: Said at farewells, graduations or when a group breaks up, to accept the parting with gentle regret, often as comfort: 别难过，天下没有不散的筵席。

cards.cue: At the farewell dinner after a year working abroad together, everyone is teary because the team will scatter to different cities next week. What do you say to comfort them?

ctx.s: 别难过了，{天下没有不散的筵席}，我们以后还会再见的。
ctx.en: Don't be sad. All good things come to an end, and we'll meet again someday.

ctx.s: 同事一个个离职，他叹了口气：“{天下没有不散的筵席}啊。”
ctx.en: As his colleagues left one after another, he sighed: "Every gathering has to break up sometime."

ctx.s: 毕业晚会上，班长说：“{天下没有不散的筵席}，祝大家前程似锦。”
ctx.en: At the graduation party the class monitor said: "Every party must end. I wish you all a bright future."

ctx.s: 你说，{天下没有不散的筵席}，我们这个小团队还能在一起多久呢？
ctx.en: Tell me, since no gathering lasts forever, how much longer can our little team stay together?

ctx.s: 乐队解散那天，主唱说{天下没有不散的筵席}，感谢大家这些年的支持。
ctx.en: The day the band split up, the singer said every gathering must end and thanked everyone for their support over the years.

ctx.s: 半个月的旅行很快过去了，{天下没有不散的筵席}，我们在机场挥手告别。
ctx.en: The fortnight's trip flew by. All good company must part, and we waved goodbye at the airport.

bad.s: 那个讨厌的同事终于走了，{天下没有不散的筵席}，太好了！
bad.en: (meant: that annoying colleague has finally left, great!)
bad.why: It expresses gentle regret at parting from good company, so it cannot be used to cheer someone's departure.

bad.s: 明天见！{天下没有不散的筵席}。
bad.en: (meant: see you tomorrow!)
bad.why: It is for a real parting, when a group breaks up for good or for a long time, not an everyday goodbye.

cards.r: yī kǒu chī bu chéng pàng zi
cards.mean: big results can't be had at one go; they come step by step
cards.lit: you can't get fat from a single mouthful

use.how: Said as advice to someone who tries to achieve too much at once, or is discouraged by slow progress: 学语言要慢慢来，一口吃不成胖子。

near.diff: 心急吃不了热豆腐 warns against impatience when you must wait; 一口吃不成胖子 says a big result is built up bit by bit, not done in one go.

cards.cue: A beginner tries to memorise the whole textbook in one weekend and feels like a failure when it doesn't stick. You remind them that progress piles up a little at a time.

ctx.s: 学外语要一点一点积累，{一口吃不成胖子}。
ctx.en: Learning a foreign language means building it up bit by bit; you can't do it all in one go.

ctx.s: 你才开始跑步就想跑全程马拉松？先从三公里跑起，{一口吃不成胖子}。
ctx.en: You've only just started running and you want to do a full marathon? Start with three kilometres; you have to build up to it.

ctx.s: 他每天背两百个单词，结果全忘了，这才明白{一口吃不成胖子}。
ctx.en: He memorised two hundred words a day and forgot the lot; only then did he see that you can't cram it all at once.

ctx.s: 教练对新队员说：“技术是一点点练出来的，{一口吃不成胖子}。”
ctx.en: The coach told the new players: "Skill is built up little by little. It doesn't happen in one go."

ctx.s: 公司刚成立，老板说：“{一口吃不成胖子}，先把第一批客户服务好。”
ctx.en: The company had just been founded, and the boss said: "We can't grow big overnight. Let's serve our first customers well."

ctx.s: 存钱买房是个长期计划，{一口吃不成胖子}，每个月存一点就行。
ctx.en: Saving for a flat is a long-term plan. It won't happen at one go; just put a bit aside each month.

bad.s: 他晚饭吃得太多了，{一口吃不成胖子}。
bad.en: (meant: he ate too much at dinner)
bad.why: It is a figure of speech about gradual progress, not a remark about how much someone actually eats.

bad.s: 他第一次创业就成功了，真是{一口吃不成胖子}。
bad.en: (meant: his very first business was a success)
bad.why: It says big results cannot come at once, so it cannot describe someone who succeeded straight away.

cards.r: xīn jí chī bu liǎo rè dòu fu
cards.mean: impatience gets you nowhere; some things have to be waited for
cards.lit: if you are impatient you can't eat hot tofu: grab it straight from the pot and you only burn your mouth

use.how: Said to calm someone who is in a hurry for a result that needs time: 别着急，心急吃不了热豆腐。 Often half-teasing.

near.diff: 一口吃不成胖子 is about results building up step by step; 心急吃不了热豆腐 is about the urge to rush and the need to wait.

cards.cue: Your friend sent off a job application this morning and has already refreshed their inbox twenty times. What do you tell them?

ctx.s: 别一直催了，快递明天才到，{心急吃不了热豆腐}。
ctx.en: Stop chasing it; the parcel won't arrive until tomorrow. Good things come to those who wait.

ctx.s: 面试结果下周才出来，你天天查也没用，{心急吃不了热豆腐}。
ctx.en: The interview results won't be out until next week; checking every day won't help. You just have to be patient.

ctx.s: 汤还要再炖一个小时，奶奶说{心急吃不了热豆腐}，让我们先去看电视。
ctx.en: The soup needed another hour, and Grandma said rushing wouldn't help and sent us off to watch TV.

ctx.s: 妈妈看他刚种下花就天天去看开没开，笑着说：“{心急吃不了热豆腐}。”
ctx.en: Seeing him check every day whether the flowers he'd just planted had bloomed, Mum laughed: "You can't hurry these things."

ctx.s: 投资要有耐心，{心急吃不了热豆腐}，涨涨跌跌很正常。
ctx.en: Investing takes patience. Impatience gets you nowhere; ups and downs are normal.

ctx.s: 他们才认识一个月，你就想让他们结婚？{心急吃不了热豆腐}啊。
ctx.en: They've only known each other a month and you want them married already? You can't rush these things.

bad.s: 快点走吧，要迟到了，{心急吃不了热豆腐}！
bad.en: (meant: hurry up, we're going to be late!)
bad.why: It warns against hurrying, so it cannot be used to urge someone to hurry.

bad.s: 他这个人很{心急吃不了热豆腐}，做什么都急。
bad.en: (meant: he is very impatient and rushes everything)
bad.why: It is a whole saying given as advice, not an adjective that can describe someone's character after hen (very).

cards.r: wàn shì kāi tóu nán
cards.mean: the beginning of anything is the hardest part
cards.lit: in all things, the start is hard

use.how: Said as a whole sentence to encourage someone, or oneself, who is struggling at the very start of something new: 别灰心，万事开头难。

near.diff: 一口吃不成胖子 warns against wanting big results at once; 万事开头难 says the first stage is the toughest and it gets easier after.

cards.cue: Your colleague has just switched careers and spends the first weeks lost and slow, wondering if it was a mistake. You tell them it will get easier once they are past this stage.

ctx.s: {万事开头难}，第一步迈出去就好了。
ctx.en: Starting is always the hardest part; once you take the first step it gets easier.

ctx.s: 刚开始学开车总会紧张，{万事开头难}嘛。
ctx.en: Everyone's nervous when they first learn to drive. The beginning is always the hardest bit.

ctx.s: 别灰心，{万事开头难}，你写完第一章就会顺了。
ctx.en: Don't lose heart. Starting is the hardest part; once you've finished the first chapter it'll flow.

ctx.s: 新店开业第一个月几乎没有客人，老板安慰自己说{万事开头难}。
ctx.en: The new shop had almost no customers in its first month, and the owner told himself that the beginning is always hardest.

ctx.s: “工作第一年很难熬吧？”“是啊，{万事开头难}，后来就慢慢习惯了。”
ctx.en: "Your first year at work must have been tough?" "Yes, the start is always the hardest. Then I gradually got used to it."

ctx.s: 她第一次一个人出国留学，什么都不懂，真是{万事开头难}。
ctx.en: The first time she went abroad to study on her own she knew nothing; the beginning really was the hardest part.

bad.s: 这个项目快结束了，最后这几天最累，真是{万事开头难}。
bad.en: (meant: the project is nearly over and these last days are the hardest)
bad.why: It says the start is the hardest part, so it cannot describe a task that is hardest at the end.

bad.s: 这道题太{万事开头难}了。
bad.en: (meant: this question is too hard)
bad.why: It is a whole saying about beginnings, not an adjective meaning difficult that can go after tai (too).

cards.r: huó dào lǎo, xué dào lǎo
cards.mean: you are never too old to learn; keep learning all your life
cards.lit: live until you are old, learn until you are old

use.how: Said as a whole sentence or after 真是 or 这叫, about someone, often older, still learning new things, or modestly about oneself after learning something.

near.diff: 学无止境 is a bookish four-character phrase saying knowledge has no limit; 活到老，学到老 is everyday and about a person going on learning at any age.

cards.cue: Your seventy-year-old neighbour has just signed up for her first English class, and the young students are surprised to see her. What saying sums up her attitude?

ctx.s: {活到老，学到老}，我今天又学到了新东西。
ctx.en: You're never too old to learn: I picked up something new again today.

ctx.s: 爸爸退休后报了书法班，真是{活到老，学到老}。
ctx.en: After retiring, Dad signed up for a calligraphy class. Never too old to learn!

ctx.s: 奶奶七十岁开始学用智能手机，她说这叫{活到老，学到老}。
ctx.en: Grandma started learning to use a smartphone at seventy; she calls it learning all your life.

ctx.s: 老教授笑着说：“{活到老，学到老}，这个软件我也得跟你们年轻人学。”
ctx.en: The old professor laughed: "We never stop learning. I have to learn this software from you young people too."

ctx.s: 现在技术变得这么快，谁不需要{活到老，学到老}呢？
ctx.en: With technology changing so fast, who doesn't need to keep learning all their life?

ctx.s: 这句话我以前一直理解错了，看来真得{活到老，学到老}。
ctx.en: I'd always misunderstood that phrase. Clearly you really do have to keep learning your whole life.

bad.s: 我爷爷八十岁了，{活到老，学到老}，什么都不想学了。
bad.en: (meant: my grandpa is eighty and doesn't want to learn anything any more)
bad.why: It praises still learning in old age, so it contradicts saying someone has stopped learning.

bad.s: 他是一个{活到老，学到老}。
bad.en: (meant: he is a lifelong learner)
bad.why: It is a saying used as a whole sentence, not a noun for a kind of person.

cards.r: jiāng shān yì gǎi, běn xìng nán yí
cards.mean: a person's basic nature hardly ever changes
cards.lit: rivers and mountains are easy to change; one's basic nature is hard to move

use.how: Said, usually with resignation or disapproval, about someone who has slipped back into a bad habit or trait despite promising to change.

cards.cue: Your cousin swore he had stopped borrowing money he never pays back, but a month later he is asking everyone for a loan again. What do you say, shaking your head?

ctx.s: 别指望他会变，{江山易改，本性难移}啊。
ctx.en: Don't expect him to change. A leopard can't change its spots.

ctx.s: 他答应不再迟到，可第二天又迟到了，真是{江山易改，本性难移}。
ctx.en: He promised never to be late again, then was late the very next day. People really don't change.

ctx.s: 她嘴上说要节约，一看到打折又买了一大堆，{江山易改，本性难移}。
ctx.en: She says she's going to save, but the moment she sees a sale she buys a pile of stuff. Old habits die hard.

ctx.s: 你真觉得他这次会改吗？俗话说{江山易改，本性难移}。
ctx.en: Do you really think he'll change this time? As the saying goes, a person's nature never really changes.

ctx.s: 结婚前她以为能改掉他的坏脾气，后来才明白{江山易改，本性难移}。
ctx.en: Before marrying she thought she could cure his bad temper; only later did she realise people's nature doesn't change.

ctx.s: 小说里的骗子换了个城市又开始骗人，作者想说的正是{江山易改，本性难移}。
ctx.en: The con man in the novel moves to another city and starts cheating people again; the author's point is exactly that a person's nature doesn't change.

bad.s: 他以前很懒，现在变得特别勤快，真是{江山易改，本性难移}。
bad.en: (meant: he used to be lazy but has become really hard-working)
bad.why: It says a person's nature does not change, so it cannot describe someone who has truly changed.

bad.s: 这座城市这些年变化很大，{江山易改，本性难移}。
bad.en: (meant: this city has changed a lot over the years)
bad.why: It is about a person's character, not about places or landscapes changing.

cards.t: 人不可貌相，海水不可斗量
cards.r: rén bù kě mào xiàng, hǎi shuǐ bù kě dǒu liáng
cards.mean: don't judge people by their looks; their worth is not seen at a glance
cards.lit: you cannot judge a person by their face, any more than you can measure the sea with a grain scoop

use.how: Said after someone unimpressive-looking turns out to be capable, or as a warning not to look down on anyone. The first half 人不可貌相 is often used alone.

near.t: 路遥知马力，日久见人心
near.diff: 路遥知马力 says time reveals a person's true character; 人不可貌相 says looks do not reveal a person's ability or worth.

cards.cue: At the chess club, everyone ignored the quiet old man in a shabby coat, until he turned out to be a former national champion.

ctx.s: 别看他穿得很普通，他可是公司老板，真是{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}。
ctx.en: Don't be fooled by his plain clothes, he owns the company. You really can't judge people by their looks.

ctx.s: 那个瘦小的女孩一上场就赢了冠军，{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}啊！
ctx.en: That slight little girl went on and won the championship. You can never tell from appearances!

ctx.s: 奶奶常对我说：“{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}，别看不起任何人。”
ctx.en: Grandma often told me: "You can't judge a person by their looks, so never look down on anyone."

ctx.s: 你怎么能凭长相就说他不行？没听说过{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}吗？
ctx.en: How can you say he's no good just from how he looks? Haven't you heard that looks tell you nothing?

ctx.s: 销售员见他穿着拖鞋没理他，谁知他买了两辆车。{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}。
ctx.en: The salesperson ignored him because he was in flip-flops, and then he bought two cars. Never judge by appearances.

ctx.s: 新来的实习生看起来很腼腆，却提出了最好的方案，大家这才明白{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}。
ctx.en: The new intern seemed shy, yet came up with the best plan, and everyone realised you can't judge people by how they look.

bad.s: 他长得很帅，{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}，大家都喜欢他。
bad.en: (meant: he is handsome, so everybody likes him)
bad.why: It warns against judging by looks; it cannot be used to say good looks make someone popular.

bad.s: 第一次见面一定要穿得体面，{人不可貌相，海水不可斗量}。
bad.en: (meant: dress well for a first meeting, because looks are what people judge you by)
bad.why: It says looks do not show a person's worth, so it cannot back up advice that appearance is what counts.

cards.r: chī yī qiàn, zhǎng yī zhì
cards.mean: every setback teaches you a lesson for next time
cards.lit: fall into a ditch once, gain a bit of wisdom

use.how: Said after a mistake or loss to draw a lesson from it, often as comfort or as a resolution: 吃一堑，长一智，下次早点准备。

near.t: 一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳
near.diff: 一朝被蛇咬 is excessive lasting fear after a bad experience; 吃一堑，长一智 is a sensible lesson that makes you wiser.

cards.cue: Your phone was stolen because you left your bag open on the metro; now you always zip it shut. What do you tell yourself?

ctx.s: 这次考试没复习好，{吃一堑，长一智}，下次我一定早点准备。
ctx.en: I didn't revise properly for this exam. Lesson learned: next time I'll start preparing early.

ctx.s: 被骗过一次以后，她再也不随便点陌生链接了，真是{吃一堑，长一智}。
ctx.en: After being scammed once, she never clicks unknown links any more. She really learned from it.

ctx.s: 爸爸安慰我：“没关系，{吃一堑，长一智}嘛。”
ctx.en: Dad comforted me: "Never mind, you live and learn."

ctx.s: 上次合同没看清就签了，亏了不少钱。{吃一堑，长一智}，这回他每一条都仔细读。
ctx.en: Last time he signed a contract without reading it and lost a lot of money. Having learned his lesson, he now reads every clause.

ctx.s: 失败并不可怕，可怕的是不懂得{吃一堑，长一智}。
ctx.en: Failure itself isn't frightening; what is frightening is not learning anything from it.

ctx.s: 创业失败后，他总结说：“{吃一堑，长一智}，这些教训比钱更值钱。”
ctx.en: After his start-up failed, he summed up: "Every setback teaches you something, and these lessons are worth more than the money."

bad.s: 他每次都犯同样的错误，真是{吃一堑，长一智}。
bad.en: (meant: he keeps making the same mistake)
bad.why: It says a setback made you wiser; repeating the same mistake is exactly the opposite.

bad.s: 我读了很多书，{吃一堑，长一智}，知识越来越丰富。
bad.en: (meant: with every book I read I know more)
bad.why: The wisdom comes from a setback or loss, not from study or reading.

cards.r: yuǎn qīn bù rú jìn lín
cards.mean: a close neighbour helps more than relatives far away
cards.lit: relatives far away are not as good as neighbours close by

use.how: Said when a neighbour helps in a moment of need, or as advice to keep good relations with neighbours. Usually stands as its own clause.

near.diff: 远水救不了近火 says any distant help comes too late; 远亲不如近邻 specifically values neighbours over far-off relatives.

cards.cue: Your parents live in another city; when a pipe burst in your flat at midnight, the family downstairs came up and helped you fix it.

ctx.s: 我家停电的时候是邻居帮的忙，{远亲不如近邻}啊。
ctx.en: When our power went out it was the neighbours who helped. A good neighbour is worth more than far-off family.

ctx.s: 老人一个人住，孩子都在国外，多亏邻居常来照顾，真是{远亲不如近邻}。
ctx.en: The old man lives alone with his children abroad; luckily his neighbours look in on him. Neighbours really count more than distant relatives.

ctx.s: 搬进新家后，妈妈说：“{远亲不如近邻}，跟邻居要处好关系。”
ctx.en: After we moved in, Mum said: "Neighbours matter more than distant relatives, so get on well with them."

ctx.s: 那天夜里爷爷突然病了，是对门的小王把他送到医院的。{远亲不如近邻}，这话一点儿不假。
ctx.en: That night Grandpa suddenly fell ill and it was Xiao Wang from across the hall who took him to hospital. It's so true that a neighbour is worth more than distant family.

ctx.s: 都说{远亲不如近邻}，你怎么连隔壁住的是谁都不知道？
ctx.en: They say a close neighbour beats far-off relatives, so how can you not even know who lives next door?

ctx.s: 楼里建了个互助群，谁家缺东西都有人送来，大家都说{远亲不如近邻}。
ctx.en: The building set up a mutual-help group, and whoever runs short of something gets it brought round. Everyone says neighbours beat distant relatives.

bad.s: 我不太喜欢我的亲戚，{远亲不如近邻}。
bad.en: (meant: I don't much like my relatives)
bad.why: It praises the practical help of neighbours nearby; it says nothing about disliking one's family.

bad.s: 他住得离公司很近，每天走路上班，{远亲不如近邻}。
bad.en: (meant: living close to work is convenient)
bad.why: It compares neighbours with distant relatives, not the convenience of living near a place.

cards.t: 世上无难事，只怕有心人
cards.r: shì shàng wú nán shì, zhǐ pà yǒu xīn rén
cards.mean: nothing is impossible if you are truly determined
cards.lit: nothing in the world is hard; it only fears the person who sets their heart on it

use.how: Said to encourage someone facing a hard task, or to praise someone who succeeded through determination. 有心人 here is a person set on a goal.

near.diff: 功夫不负有心人 looks at the reward: effort pays off; 世上无难事 stresses that no task is too hard for a determined person.

cards.cue: Your friend says that mastering Chinese characters is impossible for a foreigner, and you want to tell them that determination can overcome any task.

ctx.s: 只要你坚持练习，一定能学会。{世上无难事，只怕有心人}。
ctx.en: As long as you keep practising, you'll get it. Nothing is too hard if you set your mind to it.

ctx.s: 她五十岁才开始学钢琴，现在已经能上台演出了，真是{世上无难事，只怕有心人}。
ctx.en: She only started piano at fifty and now she performs on stage. Truly, nothing is impossible for the determined.

ctx.s: 老师在黑板上写下了一句话：“{世上无难事，只怕有心人}。”
ctx.en: The teacher wrote one line on the blackboard: "Nothing in the world is hard for those who set their hearts on it."

ctx.s: 别急着说不可能，{世上无难事，只怕有心人}，你还没真正努力过呢。
ctx.en: Don't be so quick to say it's impossible. Nothing is hard for the determined, and you haven't really tried yet.

ctx.s: 他试了几百次，终于把实验做成了。{世上无难事，只怕有心人}，这话说得没错。
ctx.en: He tried hundreds of times and finally got the experiment to work. It's true: nothing is impossible if you're determined.

ctx.s: 村民们花了十年在荒山上种满了树，正应了那句{世上无难事，只怕有心人}。
ctx.en: The villagers spent ten years covering the bare hills with trees, proving the saying that nothing is too hard for the determined.

bad.s: 这件事太难了，{世上无难事，只怕有心人}，我们放弃吧。
bad.en: (meant: this is too hard, let's give up)
bad.why: It is an encouragement to keep going; it cannot be the reason for giving up.

bad.s: 他很有心，记得每个同事的生日，{世上无难事，只怕有心人}。
bad.en: (meant: he is thoughtful and remembers everyone's birthday)
bad.why: "A person with a heart set on it" here means a determined person overcoming difficulty, not a considerate one; no hard task is involved.

cards.r: sān tiān dǎ yú, liǎng tiān shài wǎng
cards.mean: to work in fits and starts, never keeping at it
cards.lit: fish for three days, then spend two days drying the nets

story.text: The phrase is commonly traced to chapter 9 of the Qing novel Dream of the Red Chamber, where, in a slightly older wording, it describes Xue Pan: he enrolled in the family school with no real interest in study and turned up only now and then.

use.how: Used as a predicate or after 是 or 这样, criticising someone who keeps stopping and restarting a study, training or habit: 他学英语总是三天打鱼，两天晒网。

near.diff: 半途而废 is giving up halfway for good; 三天打鱼，两天晒网 is repeatedly stopping and starting without ever keeping at it.

cards.cue: All year your roommate jogs for a few days, stops for a week, starts again for a few days, then stops again, and never gets any fitter.

ctx.s: 他学英语总是{三天打鱼，两天晒网}，所以一直没什么进步。
ctx.en: He studies English in fits and starts, so he's hardly made any progress.

ctx.s: 你健身这样{三天打鱼，两天晒网}，怎么可能瘦下来？
ctx.en: If you only work out on and off like this, how are you ever going to lose weight?

ctx.s: 妈妈批评我：“练琴可不能{三天打鱼，两天晒网}。”
ctx.en: Mum told me off: "You can't practise the piano only when you feel like it."

ctx.s: 我去年办了健身卡，结果{三天打鱼，两天晒网}，一年也没去几次。
ctx.en: I got a gym card last year, but I went so irregularly that I hardly used it all year.

ctx.s: 学语言最怕{三天打鱼，两天晒网}，每天学一点比偶尔学一整天有用得多。
ctx.en: The worst thing in learning a language is doing it in fits and starts; a little every day beats a whole day now and then.

ctx.s: 他写日记从来不{三天打鱼，两天晒网}，一写就是二十年。
ctx.en: He never kept his diary on and off; he wrote in it steadily for twenty years.

bad.s: 他工作太累了，周末{三天打鱼，两天晒网}，好好休息一下。
bad.en: (meant: he works hard, so at the weekend he rests properly)
bad.why: It criticises a lack of persistence; it is not a way of describing well-earned rest.

bad.s: 他每天都坚持跑步，从不间断，真是{三天打鱼，两天晒网}。
bad.en: (meant: he runs every day without fail)
bad.why: It describes the opposite of steady persistence and is always a criticism, never praise.

cards.r: jì huà gǎn bu shàng biàn huà
cards.mean: things change faster than any plan can keep up with
cards.lit: the plan cannot catch up with the changes

use.how: A resigned comment when events upset a plan, or advice not to plan too rigidly: 本来想去爬山，结果下雨了，计划赶不上变化。

near.diff: 人算不如天算 says fate overrides human scheming, often about big outcomes; 计划赶不上变化 is about everyday plans upset by events.

cards.cue: You booked a beach holiday a month ahead, then a typhoon warning and a sudden work deadline both landed on that same week.

ctx.s: 本来想周末去爬山，结果下雨了，{计划赶不上变化}啊。
ctx.en: I'd meant to go hiking this weekend but it rained. Plans never survive what actually happens.

ctx.s: 我们早就订好了机票，可公司突然让我出差，真是{计划赶不上变化}。
ctx.en: We'd booked the flights long ago, but then work suddenly sent me on a business trip. Things just never go to plan.

ctx.s: “你不是说下个月搬家吗？”“唉，{计划赶不上变化}。”
ctx.en: "Didn't you say you were moving next month?" "Sigh, things changed."

ctx.s: 做旅行攻略可以，但别排得太满，{计划赶不上变化}，要留点余地。
ctx.en: Planning your trip is fine, but don't pack it too tight. Things never go exactly to plan, so leave some slack.

ctx.s: 项目开工前定好了时间表，没想到{计划赶不上变化}，供应商突然涨价了。
ctx.en: The schedule was fixed before the project began, but events overtook it: the supplier suddenly raised prices.

ctx.s: 他毕业时打算在北京待一辈子，可{计划赶不上变化}，后来他回老家开了家店。
ctx.en: When he graduated he meant to stay in Beijing for life, but life had other plans and he went home and opened a shop.

bad.s: 我的计划很周密，{计划赶不上变化}，一切都很顺利。
bad.en: (meant: my plan was thorough and everything went smoothly)
bad.why: It is said when events upset a plan; it cannot describe things going exactly as planned.

bad.s: 他做事从来不提前想好，所以总是{计划赶不上变化}。
bad.en: (meant: he never plans ahead, so things always go wrong)
bad.why: It blames changing circumstances, not a person's failure to plan; there must be a plan for events to overtake.

cards.r: bù pà yī wàn, jiù pà wàn yī
cards.mean: be ready for the unlikely: one rare mishap can undo everything
cards.lit: don't fear the ten thousand ordinary times; fear the one time in ten thousand

use.how: Given as the reason for taking a precaution against something unlikely: 带把伞吧，不怕一万，就怕万一。 万一 here is the rare mishap.

near.diff: 有备无患 states that being prepared prevents trouble; 不怕一万，就怕万一 stresses the rare accident you must guard against.

cards.cue: Your friend asks why you lock your bike every single time, even for a two-minute stop on a quiet street.

ctx.s: 出门还是带把伞吧，{不怕一万，就怕万一}。
ctx.en: Take an umbrella when you go out anyway. Better safe than sorry.

ctx.s: “文件已经保存了，还要备份吗？”“{不怕一万，就怕万一}，多存一份吧。”
ctx.en: "The file's saved, do I still need a backup?" "Just in case something goes wrong, save another copy."

ctx.s: 这条路虽然很安全，但{不怕一万，就怕万一}，还是要系好安全带。
ctx.en: This road is very safe, but you never know, so still buckle up.

ctx.s: 爬山前，导游让大家都带上手电筒和药品，说{不怕一万，就怕万一}。
ctx.en: Before the climb the guide had everyone bring a torch and medicine, saying it's the rare accident you have to prepare for.

ctx.s: 你别嫌麻烦，{不怕一万，就怕万一}，买份保险总没坏处。
ctx.en: Don't think of it as a hassle. It's the one-in-a-million chance that gets you, and insurance never hurts.

ctx.s: 工厂的安全检查一天也不能少，{不怕一万，就怕万一}，一次事故就可能出人命。
ctx.en: The factory's safety checks can't skip a single day. One rare slip is all it takes, and a single accident could cost a life.

bad.s: 我特别怕考试，{不怕一万，就怕万一}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm really scared of exams)
bad.why: It justifies a precaution against an unlikely mishap; it does not express a general fear.

bad.s: 万一成功了呢？{不怕一万，就怕万一}，我们试试吧。
bad.en: (meant: what if it works? Let's give it a go)
bad.why: The "one in ten thousand" in the saying is a feared mishap to guard against, not a hoped-for lucky chance.

cards.t: 一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳
cards.r: yī zhāo bèi shé yǎo, shí nián pà jǐng shéng
cards.mean: once bitten, twice shy: one bad experience leaves lasting fear
cards.lit: bitten by a snake one day, afraid of the well rope for ten years, because it looks like a snake

use.how: Said of someone whose one bad experience leaves them overly afraid of anything that resembles it, often with gentle humour or sympathy.

near.diff: 吃一堑，长一智 is a sensible lesson from a setback; 一朝被蛇咬 is lasting fear that goes beyond what is reasonable.

cards.cue: After one bout of food poisoning from a street stall years ago, your friend now refuses all street food, even from spotless vendors.

ctx.s: 他小时候被狗咬过，现在看见小狗都躲，真是{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}。
ctx.en: He was bitten by a dog as a child and now he shies away even from puppies. Once bitten, twice shy.

ctx.s: 她网购被骗过一次，从此再也不敢在网上买东西了，{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}。
ctx.en: She was cheated shopping online once and has never dared to buy anything online since. Once bitten, twice shy.

ctx.s: “你怎么连电梯都不敢坐了？”“上次被困了两个小时，{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}嘛。”
ctx.en: "How come you won't even take the lift now?" "I got stuck for two hours last time. Once bitten, twice shy."

ctx.s: 那次投资失败以后，老张{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}，连银行理财都不敢碰了。
ctx.en: After that failed investment, Lao Zhang is so gun-shy he won't even touch a bank savings product.

ctx.s: 我知道你以前被伤害过，可{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}也不是办法。
ctx.en: I know you've been hurt before, but staying afraid of everything because of it is no way to live.

ctx.s: 自从那次在海里差点出事，他{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}，连游泳池都不愿意下了。
ctx.en: Ever since his near-accident in the sea he has been so shaken that he won't even get into a swimming pool.

bad.s: 他被骗过一次，学到了教训，现在更小心了，{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}。
bad.en: (meant: he learned a sensible lesson and is now more careful)
bad.why: It describes excessive fear of harmless look-alikes, not a sensible lesson; for that, use the saying about falling into a ditch and gaining wisdom.

bad.s: 他从小就特别怕蛇，{一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳}。
bad.en: (meant: he has always been afraid of snakes)
bad.why: It is not about snakes: it describes lasting fear caused by one bad experience, not a lifelong phobia.

cards.r: zhàn zhe shuō huà bù yāo téng
cards.mean: it is easy to criticise when you don't bear the burden yourself
cards.lit: talking while standing, your back doesn't ache: the one carrying the load is the one who hurts

use.how: A blunt retort to someone who gives easy advice or criticism about a hardship they do not share: 你站着说话不腰疼。 Not for polite or formal settings.

near.diff: 饱汉不知饿汉饥 says the comfortable can't understand others' hardship; 站着说话不腰疼 attacks someone who comments glibly on it.

cards.cue: Your manager, who always leaves at five, tells the team staying until midnight that the deadline really isn't that tight.

ctx.s: 你又不用天天加班，当然觉得轻松，{站着说话不腰疼}。
ctx.en: You don't have to work overtime every day, so of course it seems easy to you. Easy for you to say.

ctx.s: “带孩子有什么难的？”“你{站着说话不腰疼}，你来带一天试试！”
ctx.en: "What's so hard about looking after kids?" "That's easy for you to say. You try doing it for a day!"

ctx.s: 他自己家里有钱，却劝我们别太在乎工资，真是{站着说话不腰疼}。
ctx.en: His own family is rich, yet he tells us not to care so much about pay. Easy for him to say.

ctx.s: 那些网友根本不了解情况，就知道{站着说话不腰疼}。
ctx.en: Those people online have no idea what it's really like; all they do is criticise from the sidelines.

ctx.s: 球迷骂球员不拼命，可他们是{站着说话不腰疼}，自己上场未必跑得动。
ctx.en: Fans slam the players for not trying, but it's easy for them to talk; they probably couldn't even run the pitch themselves.

ctx.s: 别{站着说话不腰疼}了，这活儿你来干一天就知道多累了。
ctx.en: Stop talking as if it's nothing. Do this job for a day and you'll see how exhausting it is.

bad.s: 我站了一整天，还好{站着说话不腰疼}。
bad.en: (meant: I stood all day, but luckily my back doesn't hurt)
bad.why: It is not literal; it mocks someone who talks lightly about a burden they don't carry.

bad.s: 他说得很有道理，大家都很佩服，真是{站着说话不腰疼}。
bad.en: (meant: what he said was sensible and everyone admired it)
bad.why: It is always a criticism of glib outsiders, never praise for wise words.

cards.r: jiāng hái shì lǎo de là
cards.mean: the experienced old hand still does it best
cards.lit: old ginger is still the hottest

story.text: The saying is often traced to the Southern Song official Yan Dunfu, who opposed the chancellor Qin Hui. When Qin Hui let him know that high office would follow if he gave way, Yan refused, saying he would never harm the state for his own gain, for his nature was like ginger and cassia, which grow more pungent with age. Today the saying praises experience rather than firm principle.

use.how: An exclamation or comment, often with 真是 or 啊, when an older, experienced person outdoes or outwits younger ones.

near.diff: 老马识途 is about an experienced person guiding others the right way; 姜还是老的辣 is said when the veteran outdoes the younger ones.

cards.cue: The young engineers argued for an hour over a broken machine; the old foreman walked in, listened once and fixed it in two minutes.

ctx.s: 爷爷一眼就看出车哪儿坏了，{姜还是老的辣}啊。
ctx.en: Grandpa saw what was wrong with the car at a glance. You can't beat experience.

ctx.s: 年轻人想了半天也没办法，老经理一个电话就解决了，真是{姜还是老的辣}。
ctx.en: The young staff racked their brains to no avail, and the old manager sorted it out with one phone call. The old hands still know best.

ctx.s: 比赛最后一分钟，老将一个远投锁定胜局，解说员感叹：“{姜还是老的辣}！”
ctx.en: In the last minute the veteran sealed the win with a long shot, and the commentator exclaimed: "Experience tells!"

ctx.s: 你别小看王师傅，{姜还是老的辣}，他做的菜比年轻厨师地道多了。
ctx.en: Don't underestimate Master Wang. The old hand is still the best, and his cooking is far more authentic than the young chefs'.

ctx.s: 谈判桌上，对方的小伙子被老律师问得哑口无言，{姜还是老的辣}。
ctx.en: At the negotiating table, the old lawyer's questions left the young man on the other side speechless. Experience wins out.

ctx.s: 我本来以为能瞒过奶奶，没想到她早就看穿了，{姜还是老的辣}。
ctx.en: I thought I could fool Grandma, but she had seen through me long before. You can't outwit an old hand.

bad.s: 他才二十岁就成了技术骨干，真是{姜还是老的辣}。
bad.en: (meant: he is a key engineer at only twenty)
bad.why: It praises an older, experienced person; it cannot be said of a young talent.

bad.s: 爷爷年纪大了，脾气越来越暴躁，{姜还是老的辣}。
bad.en: (meant: grandpa gets more hot-tempered with age)
bad.why: The hotness of the ginger stands for shrewdness and skill, and the saying is praise; it does not describe a bad temper.

cards.r: sài wēng shī mǎ, yān zhī fēi fú
cards.mean: a misfortune may turn out to be a blessing in disguise
cards.lit: the old man of the frontier lost his horse: who knows that it is not good fortune?

story.text: An old man on the northern frontier lost his horse when it ran off into the land of the Hu nomads. When neighbours consoled him, he said this might be good fortune. Months later the horse came back leading a fine Hu horse; when they congratulated him, he said it might be a misfortune. His son, who loved riding, fell from the new horse and broke his leg; again the old man said it might be good fortune. A year later the Hu invaded and most of the young men sent to fight were killed, but the lame son was spared, and father and son both survived.

use.how: A whole clause, often said to comfort someone after a loss or used looking back: 没考上也别难过，塞翁失马，焉知非福。 The first half, 塞翁失马, is often used alone.

near.diff: 因祸得福 states that good has already come out of a misfortune; 塞翁失马，焉知非福 says a loss may still turn out well, often before anyone knows.
车到山前必有路 says a way out will appear for a problem ahead; 塞翁失马，焉知非福 says the loss itself may prove to be a good thing.

cards.cue: Your friend lost a place on a study trip they badly wanted, and is miserable. You suggest that losing it might end up being the best thing that happened to them.

ctx.s: 没赶上那班飞机也别太难过，{塞翁失马，焉知非福}嘛。
ctx.en: Don't be too upset about missing that flight; who knows, it may turn out to be a good thing.

ctx.s: 朋友安慰她：“{塞翁失马，焉知非福}，说不定下一份工作更适合你。”
ctx.en: Her friend comforted her: "A loss can turn out to be a blessing; maybe the next job will suit you better."

ctx.s: 你说这次没被选上，会不会是{塞翁失马，焉知非福}呢？
ctx.en: Don't you think not being chosen this time might turn out to be a blessing in disguise?

ctx.s: 被裁员以后他自己开了店，生意比以前好多了，真是{塞翁失马，焉知非福}。
ctx.en: After being laid off he opened his own shop and is doing much better than before: a real blessing in disguise.

ctx.s: 那年落榜让我换了专业，没想到找到了真正喜欢的方向，{塞翁失马，焉知非福}。
ctx.en: Failing the exam that year made me change my major, and I unexpectedly found what I really love: the setback was a blessing.

ctx.s: 人生起落难料，{塞翁失马，焉知非福}，一时的得失不必看得太重。
ctx.en: Life's ups and downs are hard to predict; a loss may prove a gain, so don't take a passing setback too hard.

bad.s: 这次比赛他又赢了，真是{塞翁失马，焉知非福}。
bad.en: (meant: he won the competition again, what luck)
bad.why: The saying starts from a loss or setback; plain good fortune with no misfortune behind it does not fit.

bad.s: 我的钱包{塞翁失马，焉知非福}了，真倒霉。
bad.en: (meant: I lost my wallet, what bad luck)
bad.why: It is a complete saying, not a verb meaning to lose something, and it looks for the good side rather than complaining about bad luck.

cards.r: tiān shàng bù huì diào xiàn bǐng
cards.mean: good things don't come for free; distrust offers too good to be true
cards.lit: pies will not drop out of the sky

use.how: A whole clause used as a warning: 别信，天上不会掉馅饼。 Said about scams and offers too good to be true, or to someone hoping for gain without effort.

near.diff: 羊毛出在羊身上 says the cost of a free extra is hidden in what you pay; 天上不会掉馅饼 warns that easy gain does not exist and is likely a trap.

cards.cue: A text message says you have won a car and only need to transfer a small handling fee first. What do you tell your trusting uncle?

ctx.s: 中奖短信让你先交手续费？别信，{天上不会掉馅饼}。
ctx.en: A prize text asks you to pay a fee first? Don't believe it; nothing good falls from the sky.

ctx.s: 妈妈常说：“{天上不会掉馅饼}，想要什么就得自己去挣。”
ctx.en: Mum always says: "Nothing falls into your lap; if you want something, you have to earn it yourself."

ctx.s: 一个陌生人说能帮你轻松赚大钱，你不觉得奇怪吗？{天上不会掉馅饼}啊。
ctx.en: A stranger says he can help you make big money easily, doesn't that seem odd? Things like that don't fall from the sky.

ctx.s: 他交了押金才发现那份高薪兼职是骗局，这才明白{天上不会掉馅饼}。
ctx.en: Only after paying the deposit did he find the well-paid part-time job was a scam, and he learned that nothing comes for free.

ctx.s: 投资之前记住，{天上不会掉馅饼}，收益越高，风险往往越大。
ctx.en: Before investing, remember there's no free lunch: the higher the return, the higher the risk usually is.

ctx.s: 警方提醒市民：{天上不会掉馅饼}，不要轻易向陌生账户转账。
ctx.en: The police remind the public that offers too good to be true are traps; don't transfer money to unknown accounts.

bad.s: 我在路上捡到一百块钱，真是{天上不会掉馅饼}！
bad.en: (meant: I found a hundred yuan in the street, what a windfall!)
bad.why: It denies that windfalls happen; for an unexpected lucky gain people drop the negative and say pies fell from the sky.

bad.s: 这道数学题太难了，{天上不会掉馅饼}。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is too hard)
bad.why: It is a warning about gain without effort or offers too good to be true, not a comment on how hard something is.

cards.r: qíng rén yǎn li chū xī shī
cards.mean: to someone in love, the loved one always looks beautiful
cards.lit: in a lover's eyes appears Xishi, the famous beauty of the ancient state of Yue

use.how: A whole clause, usually teasing someone who praises the looks of a partner others find ordinary: 你觉得他帅？情人眼里出西施吧。

near.diff: 王婆卖瓜 mocks praising one's own goods or work; 情人眼里出西施 is about love making a person look beautiful to their partner.

cards.cue: Your friend keeps showing you photos of her new boyfriend and calling him the most handsome man alive, though he looks quite ordinary to you.

ctx.s: 你觉得他帅？我看是{情人眼里出西施}吧。
ctx.en: You think he's handsome? I'd say beauty is in the eye of the one in love.

ctx.s: 她男朋友长得很普通，可她总说他最好看，真是{情人眼里出西施}。
ctx.en: Her boyfriend looks very ordinary, but she always says he's the best-looking man around; love really is blind.

ctx.s: 室友笑我：“照片上那个人哪里漂亮了？{情人眼里出西施}！”
ctx.en: My roommate laughed at me: "What's so pretty about the person in that photo? You only see it because you're in love!"

ctx.s: 结婚三十年了，爷爷还夸奶奶是全村最美的，{情人眼里出西施}嘛。
ctx.en: After thirty years of marriage Grandpa still says Grandma is the prettiest woman in the village; that's love for you.

ctx.s: 别人眼里的缺点，在他看来全是可爱之处，这就叫{情人眼里出西施}。
ctx.en: Faults that others see all look charming to him; that's what being in love does.

ctx.s: 所谓{情人眼里出西施}，爱上一个人时，对方的样子往往被自己美化了。
ctx.en: As the saying goes, a lover sees a beauty: when you fall for someone, you tend to see them as better-looking than they are.

bad.s: 谈恋爱以后她变漂亮了，{情人眼里出西施}。
bad.en: (meant: she has become prettier since she started dating)
bad.why: It is about how the lover sees the loved one, not about anyone actually becoming more beautiful.

bad.s: 她是大家公认的美女，{情人眼里出西施}。
bad.en: (meant: everyone agrees she is a beauty)
bad.why: It implies the beauty is seen only by the person in love; said of someone everyone finds beautiful it makes no sense.

cards.r: mó dāo bù wù kǎn chái gōng
cards.mean: time spent preparing is not wasted; it makes the work go faster
cards.lit: sharpening the blade does not hold up the work of chopping firewood

use.how: A whole clause used to justify spending time on preparation, planning or learning before starting a task: 先把计划定好，磨刀不误砍柴工。

near.t: 工欲善其事，必先利其器
near.diff: 工欲善其事，必先利其器 is bookish and stresses having good tools; 磨刀不误砍柴工 is everyday and says time spent preparing pays for itself.
一口吃不成胖子 says big results come step by step; 磨刀不误砍柴工 says getting ready first makes the work itself quicker.

cards.cue: Your team wants to start building at once, but you insist on spending two days on a clear plan first because it will save time later.

ctx.s: 先把工具准备好再动手吧，{磨刀不误砍柴工}。
ctx.en: Let's get the tools ready before we start; preparing first won't slow us down.

ctx.s: 考试前花一天整理笔记很值得，{磨刀不误砍柴工}嘛。
ctx.en: Spending a day sorting out your notes before the exam is worth it; preparation saves time.

ctx.s: 经理说：“先花两天把计划定清楚，{磨刀不误砍柴工}。”
ctx.en: The manager said: "Let's spend two days getting the plan clear first; time spent preparing isn't wasted."

ctx.s: 你急着写代码，为什么不先把需求弄明白？{磨刀不误砍柴工}啊。
ctx.en: You're rushing to write code; why not understand the requirements first? Preparation pays off.

ctx.s: 他先花了一周学会用新软件，后来做表格比谁都快，这正是{磨刀不误砍柴工}。
ctx.en: He spent a week learning the new software first, and afterwards made spreadsheets faster than anyone: time spent preparing paid off.

ctx.s: 很多新员工觉得培训浪费时间，其实{磨刀不误砍柴工}，基础打好了，后面会顺利得多。
ctx.en: Many new staff think training wastes time, but preparation is never wasted: with a good foundation, everything after goes much more smoothly.

bad.s: 他做事拖拖拉拉，一件小事要做一整天，真是{磨刀不误砍柴工}。
bad.en: (meant: he dawdles and takes a whole day over a small task)
bad.why: It defends time spent preparing so that the work goes faster; it cannot describe someone who is simply slow.

bad.s: 他每天加班，终于升职了，{磨刀不误砍柴工}。
bad.en: (meant: he worked overtime every day and finally got promoted)
bad.why: It is about preparing before a task to work faster, not about hard work being rewarded.

cards.t: 三百六十行，行行出状元
cards.r: sān bǎi liù shí háng, háng háng chū zhuàng yuan
cards.mean: every trade or profession can produce its outstanding people
cards.lit: of the three hundred and sixty trades, every trade produces a zhuangyuan, the top scorer of the imperial exams

use.how: A whole clause, said to encourage someone in a practical or humble line of work, or to praise a master of an ordinary trade: 不上大学也能有出息，三百六十行，行行出状元。

near.diff: 是金子总会发光 says real talent will be recognised in time; 三百六十行，行行出状元 says any trade, however humble, can produce stars.

cards.cue: Your nephew wants to train as a car mechanic instead of going to university, and his parents worry it is a dead end. You reassure them.

ctx.s: 不上大学也能有出息，{三百六十行，行行出状元}。
ctx.en: You can make something of yourself without going to university; every trade has its stars.

ctx.s: 谁说送快递没前途？{三百六十行，行行出状元}嘛。
ctx.en: Who says delivering parcels has no future? Every line of work can produce outstanding people.

ctx.s: 孩子想学修车，爸爸说：“好啊，{三百六十行，行行出状元}，只要用心就行。”
ctx.en: The boy wanted to learn car repair, and his dad said: "Fine, every trade has its masters; just put your heart into it."

ctx.s: 当年家里人都反对他学厨，如今他成了全国有名的大厨，真是{三百六十行，行行出状元}。
ctx.en: His family were all against him training as a cook, and now he is a famous chef nationwide; truly, every trade can produce its champions.

ctx.s: 这次技能大赛的冠军是一位普通电工，正应了那句老话：{三百六十行，行行出状元}。
ctx.en: The winner of this skills contest is an ordinary electrician, which bears out the old saying that every trade produces its champions.

ctx.s: 报道写道：{三百六十行，行行出状元}，社会应当尊重每一种劳动。
ctx.en: The report wrote: every trade can produce outstanding people, and society should respect every kind of work.

bad.s: 他会唱歌、画画、做饭，真是{三百六十行，行行出状元}。
bad.en: (meant: he can sing, paint and cook, he's good at everything)
bad.why: It says every trade can produce top people, not that one person is good at many things.

bad.s: 他高考考了全省第一，{三百六十行，行行出状元}。
bad.en: (meant: he came first in the province in the university entrance exam)
bad.why: It says every line of work can produce top people; a top exam score is not about a trade, so it does not fit here.

cards.r: shì jīn zi zǒng huì fā guāng
cards.mean: real talent will be recognised sooner or later
cards.lit: if it is gold, it will shine sooner or later

use.how: A whole clause, often with 的 at the end, said to encourage someone whose ability is overlooked, or after such a person finally succeeds: 别灰心，是金子总会发光的。

near.t: 三百六十行，行行出状元
near.diff: 三百六十行，行行出状元 says any trade can produce stars; 是金子总会发光 says a talented person will be noticed in the end.
酒香不怕巷子深 is mostly said of good products or businesses that need no advertising; 是金子总会发光 is said of a talented person.

cards.cue: A talented colleague has been passed over for promotion again and feels nobody notices her work. You encourage her to keep going.

ctx.s: 别灰心，{是金子总会发光}，你的努力迟早有人看到。
ctx.en: Don't lose heart; real talent shines through, and someone will notice your work sooner or later.

ctx.s: 老师对落选的学生说：“{是金子总会发光}的，下次还有机会。”
ctx.en: The teacher told the student who wasn't selected: "Real talent always gets noticed in the end; there'll be another chance."

ctx.s: 你担心没人赏识你？{是金子总会发光}，先把本事练好。
ctx.en: You're worried nobody appreciates you? True talent gets recognised; first work on your skills.

ctx.s: 他在小公司默默干了好几年，终于被大公司看中了，果然{是金子总会发光}。
ctx.en: He quietly worked at a small company for years and was finally picked up by a big firm; real talent does get recognised.

ctx.s: 这位歌手在酒吧唱了十年，终于一夜成名，{是金子总会发光}啊。
ctx.en: This singer sang in bars for ten years and finally became famous overnight; talent always shines through in the end.

ctx.s: 只要有真才实学，{是金子总会发光}，不必急于一时。
ctx.en: As long as you have real ability, it will be recognised in time; there's no need to rush.

bad.s: 他买彩票中了大奖，{是金子总会发光}。
bad.en: (meant: he won the lottery jackpot)
bad.why: It is about talent being recognised; winning by pure luck has nothing to do with ability.

bad.s: 他偷东西的事{是金子总会发光}，现在大家都知道了。
bad.en: (meant: the truth about his stealing came out, and now everyone knows)
bad.why: It praises hidden talent coming to light; a secret wrongdoing being exposed is a different idea (paper can't wrap fire).

cards.r: chī rén zuǐ ruǎn, ná rén shǒu duǎn
cards.mean: accepting gifts or favours leaves you unable to say no to the giver
cards.lit: eat someone's food and your mouth goes soft; take someone's things and your hands are short

use.how: A whole clause explaining why someone cannot refuse or criticise a person who has treated them, or warning against accepting gifts: 礼物别收，吃人嘴软，拿人手短。

cards.cue: A supplier keeps inviting you to expensive dinners, and now he wants you to approve his order. Your colleague warns you why you should have declined.

ctx.s: 供应商送的礼物最好别收，{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}。
ctx.en: Better not accept gifts from suppliers; once you take something from someone, you can't say no to them.

ctx.s: 爸爸教育我：“{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}，别随便要别人的东西。”
ctx.en: Dad taught me: "Take from others and you'll owe them, so don't accept things from people lightly."

ctx.s: 你收了人家的红包，还怎么开口批评他？{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}嘛。
ctx.en: You took his red envelope, so how can you criticise him now? Accept a favour and your hands are tied.

ctx.s: 他请我吃了好几次饭，现在找我帮忙，我真不好拒绝，{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}啊。
ctx.en: He's treated me to dinner several times and now he wants a favour; I really can't refuse, I'm in his debt.

ctx.s: 评委收了选手的礼，打分自然偏向他，这就是{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}。
ctx.en: The judge accepted a gift from the contestant and naturally scored him higher; that's what accepting favours does to you.

ctx.s: 公司规定员工不得接受客户宴请，道理很简单：{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}。
ctx.en: The company forbids staff to accept dinners from clients, and the reason is simple: accept their hospitality and you can no longer say no to them.

bad.s: 她经常送朋友礼物，真是{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}。
bad.en: (meant: she often gives her friends presents, she's so generous)
bad.why: It describes the obligation of the person who receives, not the kindness of the giver.

bad.s: 他吃饭的时候说话很小声，{吃人嘴软，拿人手短}。
bad.en: (meant: he speaks softly at the dinner table)
bad.why: It is not about manners or a soft voice; it says accepting favours leaves you unable to refuse the giver.

cards.r: yáng máo chū zài yáng shēn shang
cards.mean: a seemingly free extra is really paid for by the customer
cards.lit: the wool comes from the sheep's own back

use.how: A whole clause pointing out that a gift, discount or free service is built into the price someone pays: 买一送一？羊毛出在羊身上。 Slightly sceptical in tone.

near.diff: 天上不会掉馅饼 warns that easy gain does not exist and may be a trap; 羊毛出在羊身上 explains that the cost of a freebie is hidden in your own payment.

cards.cue: A shop advertises a free kettle with every fridge, but its fridges cost more than anywhere else. Your friend is delighted; you point out the catch.

ctx.s: 买手机送耳机？{羊毛出在羊身上}，价钱早就算进去了。
ctx.en: Free earphones with the phone? You're paying for them anyway; it's already built into the price.

ctx.s: 这家店说免费送货，其实{羊毛出在羊身上}，东西比别家贵。
ctx.en: This shop says delivery is free, but the customer pays for it in the end: their goods cost more than elsewhere.

ctx.s: 你以为航空公司的免费餐是白送的？{羊毛出在羊身上}啊。
ctx.en: You think the airline's free meal is a gift? It comes out of your ticket price.

ctx.s: “买一送一”听起来划算，可{羊毛出在羊身上}，你仔细算算就明白了。
ctx.en: "Buy one get one free" sounds like a bargain, but you're the one paying for the extra; do the sums and you'll see.

ctx.s: 学校说课本免费，其实钱都加在学费里了，{羊毛出在羊身上}嘛。
ctx.en: The school says textbooks are free, but the cost has been added to the fees; the customer always pays in the end.

ctx.s: 业内人士指出，所谓“零首付”只是噱头，{羊毛出在羊身上}，利息最终都由买家承担。
ctx.en: Industry insiders point out that "no down payment" is just a gimmick: the cost comes back to the buyer, who ends up paying the interest.

bad.s: 邻居免费帮我修好了电脑，{羊毛出在羊身上}。
bad.en: (meant: my neighbour kindly fixed my computer for free)
bad.why: It says the cost of a free extra is passed back to you; about a kind neighbour's real favour it sounds like an accusation.

bad.s: 孩子长得很像爸爸，{羊毛出在羊身上}。
bad.en: (meant: the child looks just like his father)
bad.why: It is about hidden costs in a deal, not about family resemblance or children taking after their parents.

cards.r: rén féng xǐ shì jīng shen shuǎng
cards.mean: good news puts people in high spirits
cards.lit: when a person meets with a happy event, their spirits are bright and fresh

use.how: A whole clause, often teasing someone who looks radiant after a promotion, engagement or other good news: 气色这么好，人逢喜事精神爽啊。

near.diff: 笑一笑，十年少 is general advice that a cheerful habit keeps you young; 人逢喜事精神爽 describes the lift that one piece of good news gives.

cards.cue: Your colleague just got engaged and has been beaming and full of energy all week. You tease her about why she looks so lively.

ctx.s: 看你今天笑得合不拢嘴，是不是{人逢喜事精神爽}啊？
ctx.en: You can't stop smiling today; has some good news put you in high spirits?

ctx.s: 他刚升了职，走路都带风，真是{人逢喜事精神爽}。
ctx.en: He's just been promoted and walks with a spring in his step; good news really lifts the spirits.

ctx.s: 同事打趣她：“婚期定了吧？{人逢喜事精神爽}，气色这么好！”
ctx.en: A colleague teased her: "The wedding date is set, isn't it? Good news suits you, you look glowing!"

ctx.s: 爷爷抱上了孙子，{人逢喜事精神爽}，连饭都多吃了一碗。
ctx.en: Now that Grandpa has a grandson, the happy news has him in such high spirits that he even eats an extra bowl of rice.

ctx.s: 考上研究生以后，小王真是{人逢喜事精神爽}，每天早上都第一个到图书馆。
ctx.en: After getting into graduate school, Xiao Wang was in such high spirits that he was the first at the library every morning.

ctx.s: 俗话说{人逢喜事精神爽}，球队拿了冠军，队员们第二天训练格外起劲。
ctx.en: As the saying goes, good news lifts the spirits: after winning the title, the players trained with extra energy the next day.

bad.s: 每天早上跑步让我{人逢喜事精神爽}。
bad.en: (meant: running every morning makes me feel refreshed)
bad.why: The lift must come from a happy event such as good news, not from a habit like exercise.

bad.s: 她昨天{人逢喜事精神爽}了一份新工作。
bad.en: (meant: she happily got a new job yesterday)
bad.why: It is a complete saying, not a verb that takes an object; state the good news first, then add the saying as a comment.

cards.r: xiào yi xiào, shí nián shào
cards.mean: laughing often keeps you young
cards.lit: laugh a little, and you are ten years younger

use.how: A whole clause, said to cheer someone up or as homely health advice about keeping a cheerful mood: 别老皱着眉头，笑一笑，十年少。

near.diff: 人逢喜事精神爽 describes high spirits after one piece of good news; 笑一笑，十年少 recommends laughing as a habit for health and youth.

cards.cue: Your grandmother is eighty, still full of energy, and jokes with her neighbours every day. What does she say is her secret?

ctx.s: 别老皱着眉头，{笑一笑，十年少}嘛。
ctx.en: Don't keep frowning; laughing keeps you young, you know.

ctx.s: 你最近怎么总是愁眉苦脸的？{笑一笑，十年少}，开心点儿。
ctx.en: Why have you looked so miserable lately? A smile takes years off you; cheer up.

ctx.s: 奶奶每天跟邻居说说笑笑，身体一直很好，她总说{笑一笑，十年少}。
ctx.en: Grandma chats and laughs with the neighbours every day and is in very good health; she always says laughter keeps you young.

ctx.s: 公园里一群老人每天早上聚在一起放声大笑，说这叫{笑一笑，十年少}。
ctx.en: In the park a group of old people get together every morning to laugh out loud; they say laughing keeps you young.

ctx.s: 医生建议老人多参加集体活动，保持好心情，{笑一笑，十年少}。
ctx.en: The doctor advised older people to join group activities and stay in a good mood, since laughter keeps you young.

ctx.s: 常言道{笑一笑，十年少}，乐观的心态对健康大有好处。
ctx.en: As the saying goes, laughing keeps you young: an optimistic outlook does a great deal for your health.

bad.s: 他摔了一跤，大家都{笑一笑，十年少}。
bad.en: (meant: he fell over and everyone laughed at him)
bad.why: It is advice to keep a cheerful mood for health, not a description of people laughing at something.

bad.s: 我哥哥{笑一笑，十年少}，看起来比我还小。
bad.en: (meant: my older brother looks younger than me)
bad.why: It is a saying recommending laughter, not a description of someone who looks young; it cannot stand in as a predicate like that.

cards.r: hèn tiě bù chéng gāng
cards.mean: to be exasperated that someone you care about won't do better
cards.lit: to resent iron for not turning into steel: the raw material is there, but it will not become what it could be

use.how: Usually a predicate or after 是/真是: 我是恨铁不成钢. Said by parents, teachers or older relatives about someone they care for who wastes their potential.

near.diff: 望子成龙 is the hope that a child will succeed; 恨铁不成钢 is the frustration when they fall short of it.

cards.cue: A teacher shouts at a bright student who keeps skipping homework, then explains that she only gets angry because she knows how good he could be.

ctx.s: 爸爸骂你，是{恨铁不成钢}，不是不爱你。
ctx.en: When Dad scolds you, it's because he's frustrated you're not doing better, not because he doesn't love you.

ctx.s: 看着弟弟整天打游戏不复习，姐姐真是{恨铁不成钢}。
ctx.en: Watching her brother play games all day instead of revising, his sister was beside herself with frustration.

ctx.s: 老师说：“你这么聪明，却总不用功，我是{恨铁不成钢}啊！”
ctx.en: The teacher said: "You're so clever, but you never work hard. It drives me mad because I know what you could do!"

ctx.s: 教练对那个天赋最好的球员最严厉，大家都明白他是{恨铁不成钢}。
ctx.en: The coach was hardest on the most talented player, and everyone understood he was frustrated to see that talent wasted.

ctx.s: 妈妈说话虽然难听，可那种{恨铁不成钢}的心情，我后来才懂。
ctx.en: Mum's words were harsh, but it was only later that I understood how frustrated she was that I wasn't living up to my potential.

ctx.s: 他一次次失业又不肯学新技术，朋友们对他都有点{恨铁不成钢}。
ctx.en: He lost job after job and still refused to learn new skills; his friends were exasperated with him.

bad.s: 那个陌生人插队，我{恨铁不成钢}，跟他吵了起来。
bad.en: (meant: a stranger jumped the queue, I was furious and argued with him)
bad.why: It is the frustration of caring about someone who could do better, not anger at a stranger's bad behaviour.

bad.s: 我的手机又坏了，真让我{恨铁不成钢}。
bad.en: (meant: my phone broke again, it really annoys me)
bad.why: It is said about a person whose potential is being wasted, not about a faulty object or bad luck.

cards.r: tuì yī bù hǎi kuò tiān kōng
cards.mean: giving way in a quarrel brings peace of mind
cards.lit: take one step back and the sea is wide and the sky boundless: stepping back opens up a vast view

use.how: Quoted as advice, often after 忍一时风平浪静: 算了吧，退一步海阔天空. Said to calm someone in a dispute or persuade them to let a grudge go.

near.diff: 退避三舍 is to back right off and avoid any confrontation with someone; 退一步海阔天空 is advice that letting a quarrel go brings peace.

cards.cue: Your friend is still furious, a week later, about a neighbour who parked in her space once. You tell her that letting it go will make her feel much better.

ctx.s: 为这点小事吵什么？{退一步海阔天空}嘛。
ctx.en: Why argue over such a small thing? Let it go and you'll feel a lot better.

ctx.s: 忍一时风平浪静，{退一步海阔天空}。
ctx.en: Hold your temper for a moment and the storm passes; take a step back and the whole world opens up.

ctx.s: 跟邻居闹到这个地步，何必呢？{退一步海阔天空}。
ctx.en: Why let things with the neighbours get this bad? Give a little and you'll both have peace.

ctx.s: 他本想跟同事争到底，后来想通了，{退一步海阔天空}。
ctx.en: He had meant to fight his colleague to the bitter end, but then he saw sense: giving way would bring him peace.

ctx.s: 奶奶常说：“夫妻之间别太较真，{退一步海阔天空}。”
ctx.en: Grandma always says: "Between husband and wife, don't be so stubborn; give way a little and life is easier."

ctx.s: 那件事过去这么久了，你还放不下吗？有时候{退一步海阔天空}。
ctx.en: That was so long ago and you still can't let it go? Sometimes stepping back is what sets you free.

bad.s: 敌人太强了，我们只好{退一步海阔天空}，先撤到山里。
bad.en: (meant: the enemy was too strong, so we had to retreat to the hills for now)
bad.why: It is advice about letting go of a quarrel or grudge for one's own peace, not a description of a military or tactical retreat.

bad.s: 今天放假，天气很好，真是{退一步海阔天空}！
bad.en: (meant: it's a holiday and the weather is great, how open and free I feel!)
bad.why: It is about yielding in a conflict, not about nice weather or a relaxed mood.

cards.r: cǐ dì wú yín sān bǎi liǎng
cards.mean: a clumsy denial that gives away the very thing it hides
cards.lit: here there are no three hundred taels of silver: a sign that points straight to the hidden treasure

story.text: A man named Zhang San buried his three hundred taels of silver and, afraid someone would find it, put up a sign over the spot: here there are no three hundred taels of silver. His neighbour Wang Er read the sign, dug up the silver and, afraid in turn of being suspected, put up his own sign: neighbour Wang Er did not steal it.

use.how: Usually a predicate after 是/简直是/有点: 你这样解释，不是此地无银三百两吗？ Mocks a denial or cover-up that exposes what it tries to hide.

near.diff: 欲盖弥彰 is the bookish chengyu for a cover-up making things worse; 此地无银三百两 is the everyday, more mocking saying.

cards.cue: Before anyone has asked, your flatmate announces loudly that he definitely did not eat the last piece of your birthday cake. His mouth has cream on it.

ctx.s: 没人问你，你就说自己没偷看，这不是{此地无银三百两}吗？
ctx.en: Nobody asked you, and you say you didn't peek? That's as good as admitting it.

ctx.s: 他一进门就说“我可没去网吧”，简直是{此地无银三百两}。
ctx.en: The moment he walked in he said "I definitely wasn't at the internet café", which gave the game away completely.

ctx.s: 公司突然发声明说财务没问题，大家反而觉得有点{此地无银三百两}。
ctx.en: The company suddenly issued a statement saying its finances were fine, which only made people suspect they weren't.

ctx.s: 你越解释越像{此地无银三百两}，还是别说了。
ctx.en: The more you explain, the more it sounds like a confession. Better stop talking.

ctx.s: 她在门上贴了张纸条：“抽屉里没有日记。”真是{此地无银三百两}。
ctx.en: She stuck a note on the door: "There is no diary in the drawer." She might as well have pointed to it.

ctx.s: “我跟她只是普通朋友，真的，绝对普通！”“好了，别{此地无银三百两}了。”
ctx.en: "She and I are just friends, honestly, totally just friends!" "All right, stop, you're giving yourself away."

bad.s: 他很穷，家里真是{此地无银三百两}。
bad.en: (meant: he is poor, there is really no money in his house)
bad.why: It is not about having no money; it mocks a denial that reveals the truth it tries to hide.

bad.s: 我把钱藏得很好，谁也找不到，真是{此地无银三百两}。
bad.en: (meant: I hid the money so well that nobody can find it)
bad.why: It means a hiding attempt that fails by drawing attention, never one that succeeds.

cards.r: wáng pó mài guā, zì mài zì kuā
cards.mean: to sing the praises of one's own goods or work
cards.lit: old Mrs Wang sells melons and praises the melons she is selling

use.how: Teasing others who praise their own things, or modest self-mockery: 不是我王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸，这菜真好吃. Often shortened to 王婆卖瓜.

near.diff: 自吹自擂 is a sharper criticism of boasting in general; 王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸 is lighter and is about praising one's own goods or work.

cards.cue: You cooked dinner for friends and want to say it turned out delicious, while admitting with a laugh that the cook is hardly a neutral judge.

ctx.s: 不是我{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}，我做的饺子真的很好吃。
ctx.en: I know I'm biased, but my dumplings really are delicious.

ctx.s: 老板说自己的茶是全城最好的，这不就是{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}吗？
ctx.en: The shop owner says his tea is the best in town. Well, he would say that, wouldn't he?

ctx.s: 他总在朋友圈夸自己的画，大家笑他{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}。
ctx.en: He keeps praising his own paintings online, and everyone teases him for blowing his own trumpet.

ctx.s: 广告里每家都说自己的产品最好，都是{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}。
ctx.en: In the ads every company claims its product is the best; naturally they all praise their own goods.

ctx.s: 我就{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}一回：这次的设计方案是我最满意的。
ctx.en: Let me blow my own trumpet just this once: this design is the one I'm proudest of.

ctx.s: 作者在序言里笑称，自己夸这本书难免有点{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}。
ctx.en: In the preface the author jokes that his praising his own book is bound to sound like self-promotion.

bad.s: 李奶奶自己种瓜，{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}，不经过中间商。
bad.en: (meant: Granny Li grows her own melons and sells them herself, with no middleman)
bad.why: It is not about selling your own produce directly; it means praising your own goods or work.

bad.s: 老师在全班面前{王婆卖瓜，自卖自夸}，表扬了我的作文。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher praised my essay in front of the class)
bad.why: It is praising one's own goods or work, not praising someone else's.

cards.r: qiāng dǎ chū tóu niǎo
cards.mean: whoever stands out from the crowd is the first to be attacked
cards.lit: the gun shoots the bird that sticks its head out first

use.how: Quoted as a warning or explanation: 别太张扬，枪打出头鸟. Said of people who speak up, show off or lead and so draw criticism or trouble.

near.diff: 树大招风 is about the rich or famous attracting envy; 枪打出头鸟 is about whoever first speaks up or stands out being targeted.

cards.cue: At a meeting everyone grumbles in private about the new rule, but nobody wants to be the first to object to the boss's face.

ctx.s: 新来的别太张扬，{枪打出头鸟}。
ctx.en: When you're new, don't make yourself conspicuous: the one who sticks out gets shot down.

ctx.s: 大家都不满意，可谁都不肯先开口，怕{枪打出头鸟}。
ctx.en: Everyone was unhappy, but nobody would speak first, afraid of being the one who gets targeted.

ctx.s: 他第一个提出反对意见，结果被领导批评了，真是{枪打出头鸟}。
ctx.en: He was the first to object and ended up being criticised by the management. The one who stands out always takes the hit.

ctx.s: 妈妈提醒我：“在单位里少出风头，{枪打出头鸟}啊。”
ctx.en: Mum reminded me: "Don't try to stand out at work. The bird that sticks its head out is the one that gets shot."

ctx.s: 第一家降价的店马上被同行围攻，这就叫{枪打出头鸟}。
ctx.en: The first shop to cut its prices was immediately attacked by all its competitors. That's what happens to whoever goes first.

ctx.s: 很多人不敢创新，就是因为相信{枪打出头鸟}这句话。
ctx.en: Many people don't dare to innovate precisely because they believe that whoever stands out gets struck down.

bad.s: 小偷被警察抓住了，真是{枪打出头鸟}。
bad.en: (meant: the thief was caught by the police, he got what he deserved)
bad.why: It is about someone being attacked for standing out, not about a wrongdoer being justly punished.

bad.s: 他跑步跑在最前面，第一个到了终点，真是{枪打出头鸟}！
bad.en: (meant: he ran at the front and finished first, how impressive)
bad.why: It is a warning that standing out brings trouble, never praise for being first.

cards.r: wù yǐ lèi jù, rén yǐ qún fēn
cards.mean: birds of a feather flock together: people keep to their own kind
cards.lit: things gather by kind, people divide into groups

story.text: The saying goes back to a line in the Xici commentary to the Book of Changes, which says that kinds gather by kind and things divide into groups. The modern saying reshapes that line into a pair about things and people.

use.how: Quoted as a full sentence to explain why people of a type are found together; often implies judging someone by their friends, sometimes disapprovingly.

near.diff: 近朱者赤，近墨者黑 says company changes you; 物以类聚，人以群分 says similar people find each other in the first place.

cards.cue: You notice that your cousin's new friends are all, like him, obsessed with motorbikes and always late for everything. Of course they found each other.

ctx.s: 他的朋友个个爱读书，真是{物以类聚，人以群分}。
ctx.en: Every one of his friends loves reading. Birds of a feather really do flock together.

ctx.s: {物以类聚，人以群分}，看看他跟谁来往，就知道他是什么样的人。
ctx.en: People keep to their own kind: look at who he spends time with and you'll know what he's like.

ctx.s: 我每次说起新男朋友，妈妈总先问他交的是什么朋友，她信{物以类聚，人以群分}。
ctx.en: Whenever I mention a new boyfriend, Mum first asks what kind of friends he has; she believes people keep to their own kind.

ctx.s: 公司里爱运动的人慢慢成了一个小圈子，这就是{物以类聚，人以群分}吧。
ctx.en: The people at work who love sport gradually formed their own little circle. Like attracts like, I suppose.

ctx.s: 我们几个都是夜猫子，难怪能成为好朋友，{物以类聚，人以群分}嘛。
ctx.en: We're all night owls, no wonder we became close friends. Birds of a feather, after all.

ctx.s: 有了网络，兴趣相同的人更容易走到一起，“{物以类聚，人以群分}”这话一点不假。
ctx.en: With the internet, people with the same interests find each other more easily. It's quite true that like attracts like.

bad.s: 我们性格完全相反，却成了好朋友，真是{物以类聚，人以群分}。
bad.en: (meant: we are total opposites but became good friends)
bad.why: It says similar people gather together; for opposites becoming friends it is exactly the wrong saying.

bad.s: 超市把水果和蔬菜放在一起卖，这叫{物以类聚，人以群分}。
bad.en: (meant: the supermarket displays fruit and vegetables together)
bad.why: Despite mentioning things, the saying is about people and their companions, not about how goods are arranged.

cards.r: dāng jú zhě mí, páng guān zhě qīng
cards.mean: onlookers see clearly what those involved cannot
cards.lit: the player in the game is confused, the one watching from the side sees clearly

use.how: Quoted as a full sentence, often to justify giving or seeking an outsider's view: 当局者迷，旁观者清，你听听朋友的意见吧.

near.t: 不识庐山真面目，只缘身在此山中
near.diff: The poem line describes not seeing the whole while inside it; 当局者迷，旁观者清 adds that an outsider can see it and is the one quoted in advice.

cards.cue: Everyone except your friend can see that her boyfriend is using her, and you want to persuade her to trust the view of people outside the relationship.

ctx.s: 你自己看不出来，我们可看得很清楚，{当局者迷，旁观者清}嘛。
ctx.en: You can't see it yourself, but we can see it very clearly. The people watching always see more.

ctx.s: {当局者迷，旁观者清}，你还是听听朋友们怎么说吧。
ctx.en: Those involved are the last to see clearly. You should listen to what your friends are saying.

ctx.s: 写完论文最好请别人读一遍，{当局者迷，旁观者清}，别人更容易发现问题。
ctx.en: Once you've written your thesis, get someone else to read it; an outsider spots the problems you can't.

ctx.s: 他俩吵了半天也没结果，最后还是同事一句话点醒了他们，真是{当局者迷，旁观者清}。
ctx.en: They argued for ages and got nowhere; in the end a colleague's single remark opened their eyes. Outsiders really do see more clearly.

ctx.s: 公司请外部顾问，就是因为{当局者迷，旁观者清}。
ctx.en: The company hired outside consultants precisely because those inside can't see what an outsider can.

ctx.s: “你觉得我该不该辞职？”“{当局者迷，旁观者清}，我说说我的看法吧。”
ctx.en: "Do you think I should quit?" "You're too close to it. Let me tell you how it looks from outside."

bad.s: 我站在路边看热闹，{当局者迷，旁观者清}，觉得很好玩。
bad.en: (meant: I stood at the roadside watching the fuss and found it fun)
bad.why: It is not about enjoying the show as a bystander; it says the outsider understands a situation better than those caught up in it.

bad.s: 这道数学题太难了，我{当局者迷，旁观者清}，怎么也做不出来。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is too hard, I just can't solve it)
bad.why: It needs two sides, someone involved and an onlooker who sees better; it is not a way of saying something is hard or confusing.

cards.r: yī cùn guāng yīn yī cùn jīn
cards.mean: time is as precious as gold; don't waste it
cards.lit: an inch of time is an inch of gold

story.text: The line comes from a poem written at the White Deer Grotto, a famous place of study, by the late Tang poet Wang Zhenbai: so absorbed in his books that he had not noticed spring was far advanced, he wrote that every inch of time is an inch of gold. Today it is often followed by a later line: an inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

use.how: Quoted as a full sentence, typically by parents and teachers urging the young to study and not waste time; often paired with 寸金难买寸光阴.

near.diff: 光阴似箭 says time flies past quickly; 一寸光阴一寸金 says time is precious and must be used well.

cards.cue: A grandfather finds his grandson lying on the sofa scrolling his phone the week before exams and reminds him how valuable every hour is.

ctx.s: {一寸光阴一寸金}，别再浪费时间了。
ctx.en: Time is precious, stop wasting it.

ctx.s: 教室墙上写着：“{一寸光阴一寸金}，寸金难买寸光阴。”
ctx.en: On the classroom wall it says: "An inch of time is an inch of gold, and gold can't buy back an inch of time."

ctx.s: 爷爷常对我说{一寸光阴一寸金}，年轻时要多读书。
ctx.en: Grandpa often tells me that time is worth more than gold and that I should read a lot while I'm young.

ctx.s: 离考试只剩一个月了，真是{一寸光阴一寸金}啊。
ctx.en: There's only a month left before the exam; every minute counts now.

ctx.s: 退休以后他才明白{一寸光阴一寸金}的道理，开始学画画。
ctx.en: Only after he retired did he really understand how precious time is, and he started learning to paint.

ctx.s: 你整个假期都在睡觉，难道不知道{一寸光阴一寸金}吗？
ctx.en: You've slept through the whole holiday. Don't you know time is precious?

bad.s: 这个手表很贵，真是{一寸光阴一寸金}。
bad.en: (meant: this watch is very expensive)
bad.why: It is about the value of time itself, not about the price of a clock, watch or anything made of gold.

bad.s: 他家很有钱，真是{一寸光阴一寸金}。
bad.en: (meant: his family is very rich)
bad.why: The gold is only a measure of how precious time is; the saying has nothing to do with wealth.

cards.t: 路遥知马力，日久见人心
cards.r: lù yáo zhī mǎ lì, rì jiǔ jiàn rén xīn
cards.mean: only time shows what a person is really like
cards.lit: a long road shows a horse's strength, long days show a person's heart

use.how: Quoted as a full sentence, often the second half alone (日久见人心), about learning over time whether someone is sincere, loyal or false.

near.t: 人不可貌相，海水不可斗量
near.diff: 人不可貌相 warns against judging by looks at first sight; 路遥知马力，日久见人心 says the truth about a person shows only over a long time.

cards.cue: The quiet colleague nobody trusted at first has stood by you through two hard years, while your charming friend vanished. Now you know who is true.

ctx.s: 你现在不相信我没关系，{路遥知马力，日久见人心}。
ctx.en: It's fine if you don't believe me now. In time you'll see what kind of person I am.

ctx.s: {路遥知马力，日久见人心}，交朋友要慢慢来，时间长了才知道谁靠得住。
ctx.en: Only time shows what someone is really like: take your time making friends, and in the long run you'll learn who can be relied on.

ctx.s: 刚结婚时婆婆对她不放心，十年过去了，{路遥知马力，日久见人心}。
ctx.en: When she first married, her mother-in-law didn't trust her; ten years on, time had shown what she was really like.

ctx.s: 公司困难时，留下来的都是靠得住的人，真是{路遥知马力，日久见人心}。
ctx.en: When the company hit hard times, the ones who stayed were the reliable ones. Time really does show people's true colours.

ctx.s: 他当初的热情都是装出来的，{路遥知马力，日久见人心}，后来大家都看清了。
ctx.en: His early warmth was all an act; as time went on, everyone saw through him.

ctx.s: “你怎么知道他是真心的？”“{路遥知马力，日久见人心}，我们认识二十年了。”
ctx.en: "How do you know he's sincere?" "Time tells you who people are, and we've known each other for twenty years."

bad.s: 我第一次见他就{路遥知马力，日久见人心}，知道他是好人。
bad.en: (meant: the first time I met him I knew he was a good person)
bad.why: The whole point is that it takes a long time to know someone; it cannot describe a first impression.

bad.s: 这辆车跑了十万公里还没坏，真是{路遥知马力，日久见人心}。
bad.en: (meant: this car has done a hundred thousand kilometres and never broken down)
bad.why: The horse is only the image; the saying is about a person's character, not a machine's durability.

cards.r: jiā jiā yǒu běn nán niàn de jīng
cards.mean: every family has troubles that outsiders don't see
cards.lit: every household has its own scripture that is hard to chant

use.how: Quoted as a full sentence to console someone or to stop envying or judging another family: 别羡慕别人了，家家有本难念的经.

near.diff: 清官难断家务事 says outsiders can't judge family quarrels; 家家有本难念的经 says every family has hidden troubles.

cards.cue: Your friend envies the neighbours with their big house and smiling photos, but you know they are struggling with a sick parent and money worries.

ctx.s: 别羡慕他们了，{家家有本难念的经}。
ctx.en: Don't envy them. Every family has its own troubles.

ctx.s: 看起来他家什么都好，其实{家家有本难念的经}啊。
ctx.en: Their family looks perfect from outside, but every household has problems you don't see.

ctx.s: 听完邻居的诉苦，妈妈叹了口气：“唉，{家家有本难念的经}。”
ctx.en: After listening to the neighbour's woes, Mum sighed: "Ah, every family has its burdens."

ctx.s: 同事们聚餐时互相倒苦水，有的为老人看病发愁，有的为孩子上学操心，真是{家家有本难念的经}。
ctx.en: Over dinner my colleagues swapped complaints: one was worried about an elderly parent's treatment, another about a child's schooling. Every family really does have its troubles.

ctx.s: 朋友抱怨孩子不听话，我笑着说：“{家家有本难念的经}，我家也一样。”
ctx.en: My friend complained that her child won't listen. I laughed: "Every family has its troubles; it's the same in mine."

ctx.s: 节目里那些看似幸福的明星也有家庭烦恼，看来{家家有本难念的经}。
ctx.en: Even the celebrities who look so happy on the show have family worries. It seems every family has its troubles.

bad.s: 和尚每天都要{家家有本难念的经}，非常辛苦。
bad.en: (meant: monks have to chant difficult sutras every day)
bad.why: The scripture is only an image; the saying is about families' hidden troubles, not about real religious chanting.

bad.s: 这本英语课本太难了，真是{家家有本难念的经}。
bad.en: (meant: this English textbook is really hard)
bad.why: It is not about a book being hard to read; it means every household has private difficulties.

cards.r: qiān lǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zú xià
cards.mean: every great undertaking begins with a single first step
cards.lit: a journey of a thousand li starts from the ground beneath your feet

story.text: The line comes from chapter sixty-four of the Daodejing, attributed to Laozi, in a run of three images: a tree too big to put your arms around grows from a tiny shoot, a terrace nine storeys high rises from heaps of earth, and a journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet. The point is that great things grow from small beginnings.

use.how: Quoted whole to urge someone to stop dreaming or planning and take the first concrete step towards a big goal: 别光想了，千里之行，始于足下。

near.diff: 万事开头难 says the start is the hardest part; 千里之行，始于足下 urges you to make that start, however small.
一口吃不成胖子 warns against expecting results at once; 千里之行，始于足下 tells you to begin now with one step.
